title: Charges Dropped for Trump Co-Defendants Walt Nauta and Carlos De Oliveira
synopsis: On January 29, 2025, the Trump Justice Department moved to dismiss all criminal charges against Walt Nauta, Trump's personal valet, and Carlos De Oliveira, a Mar-a-Lago property manager, who had been indicted for allegedly helping Trump obstruct an FBI investigation into the hoarding of classified documents. The 11th Circuit Court of Appeals formally granted the dismissal on February 11, 2025, ending the final remnant of special counsel Jack Smith's federal criminal investigations. Both men had been charged with conspiring to hide documents from the FBI. The charges were dropped days after the DOJ fired the career prosecutors who built the case. Critics noted that DOJ officials had just stated no one could be trusted who worked on the Trump prosecutions, making dismissal of allied defendants a logical extension of that position. The move erased the legal jeopardy of two individuals who pleaded not guilty to obstruction.

sources.title: US court drops documents case against Trump associates, final step in legal saga

title: DOJ Pattern of Dropping Cases Against Trump-Aligned Figures
synopsis: Within the first month of Trump's return to office, the Justice Department established a pattern of abandoning cases against individuals with ties or usefulness to the president. By February 2025, prosecutors dropped a case against former Republican Rep. Jeff Fortenberry of Nebraska; withdrew from an investigation into Republican Rep. Andy Ogles of Tennessee, who had introduced a bill allowing Trump to seek a third term; and moved to dismiss corruption charges against New York Mayor Eric Adams, a Democrat who had signaled cooperation with Trump's immigration crackdown. Seven prosecutors in the Adams case resigned rather than carry out what they characterized as an unlawful quid pro quo. Former DOJ officials said the department appeared to be cutting breaks to political allies while preparing to use its powers against perceived enemies. Harvard law professor Jack Goldsmith characterized the pattern as doublespeak and a playbook to weaponize DOJ like never before.

sources.title: Is the Justice Department cutting breaks to people who seem loyal to Trump? : NPR

title: Eric Adams Corruption Charges Dropped in Exchange for Immigration Cooperation
synopsis: In February 2025, the Trump DOJ directed federal prosecutors in New York to drop corruption charges against Democratic NYC Mayor Eric Adams. Acting Deputy AG Emil Bove's memo stated the September 2024 indictment — charging Adams with accepting bribes from Turkish officials — was interfering with Adams' capacity to support Trump's immigration crackdown and his 2025 re-election campaign. Eight federal prosecutors resigned in protest, describing the move as an unlawful quid pro quo. U.S. Attorney for Manhattan Danielle Sassoon also resigned rather than comply, writing that Bove had designs on dropping charges before their conversation. In a 78-page ruling on April 2, 2025, U.S. District Judge Dale Ho dismissed the case with prejudice, writing that the DOJ's rationale smacks of a bargain: dismissal of the indictment in exchange for immigration policy concessions, and found the pressure disturbing. The dismissal with prejudice meant prosecutors could not refile after the mayoral election.

sources.title: Prosecutors file motion to drop corruption charges against NYC Mayor Eric Adams - CBS New York

title: Trump Fires FEC Chair Weintraub, Paralyzing Campaign Finance Enforcement
synopsis: On January 31, 2025, President Trump sent a letter to Federal Election Commission Commissioner and Chair Ellen Weintraub stating You are hereby removed as a Member of the Federal Election Commission, effective immediately. Weintraub, who had served since 2002 after appointment by George W. Bush, declared the firing illegal under the Federal Election Campaign Act. Combined with two prior vacancies — Republican Sean Cooksey's January resignation and Allen Dickerson's April 30, 2025 resignation — the FEC dropped to three commissioners, losing the four-member quorum required for enforcement actions, advisory opinions, and rulemaking. This was only the fourth quorum loss in FEC history. The agency charged with policing campaign finance laws was effectively paralyzed during a period when Trump allies were raising unprecedented political funds. Democrats sued to block Trump's executive order asserting White House control over independent agencies including the FEC.

sources.title: Democratic FEC Chair Ellen Weintraub says Trump fired her. She says it's not legal. - CBS News

title: Trump Executive Order Subjugating All Independent Regulatory Agencies
synopsis: On February 18, 2025, Trump signed an executive order placing all independent federal regulatory agencies — including the FEC, SEC, FTC, NLRB, and others — under direct White House budgetary and policy control, requiring all executive branch officials to defer to Trump's own interpretation of the law. Congress established these agencies as independent precisely to insulate them from political pressure, following the Watergate era. The order empowered the White House to shift funding and override policy decisions at the Federal Election Commission, Securities and Exchange Commission, National Labor Relations Board, and more than a dozen other bodies. The Democratic National Committee sued in February 2025, arguing the order could weaponize the FEC against political opponents. Legal scholars characterized the order as the most sweeping claim of executive authority over independent agencies in American history, potentially dismantling a century of regulatory independence.

sources.title: Trump claims expanded power over independent agencies : NPR

title: Trump Fires FTC Democratic Commissioners Bedoya and Slaughter
synopsis: On March 18, 2025, Trump fired both Democratic commissioners of the Federal Trade Commission — Alvaro Bedoya and Rebecca Kelly Slaughter — in an unprecedented move to seize control of the antitrust and consumer protection agency. Both commissioners declared the firings illegal and filed suit. Commissioner Bedoya stated: This is corruption plain and simple. On July 17, 2025, U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan ruled Trump's firing of Slaughter was illegal, citing nearly a century of Supreme Court precedent protecting FTC commissioners from at-will removal. The judge wrote that for-cause removal protections remain constitutional, as they have for almost a century. The firings removed the last Democratic opposition within the five-member FTC, giving the Trump administration effective control over all antitrust enforcement — during a period when Musk's companies faced potential scrutiny.

sources.title: Trump fires 2 Democrats on the Federal Trade Commission, seeking more control over regulators | AP News

title: Trump Fires NLRB Members, Paralyzing Labor Enforcement Agency
synopsis: On January 28, 2025, Trump fired two Democratic National Labor Relations Board officials: board member Gwynne Wilcox, whose term ran until August 2028, and General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo. The removal of Wilcox was described by labor law experts as unprecedented in the agency's history and potentially a violation of federal labor law. With two pre-existing vacancies, the loss of Wilcox left the NLRB with only two members — far short of the three-member quorum needed to decide cases. Hundreds of pending cases accusing companies of unlawful labor practices were brought to a standstill. Abruzzo, who served as the agency's prosecutor, had aggressively pursued worker protections during the Biden years. The dual firing effectively rendered the NLRB unable to enforce labor law and paved the way for Republican-only control of the board, benefiting major corporations facing union organizing and unfair labor practice charges.

sources.title: Trump paralyzes US labor board by firing Democratic member

title: DOJ Weaponization Working Group Targets Trump Prosecutors
synopsis: On February 5, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi issued a memo establishing a Weaponization Working Group purportedly to root out abuses of the criminal justice process. The group was tasked with reviewing special counsel Jack Smith's prosecutions of Trump, Manhattan DA Alvin Bragg's hush-money case, and New York AG Letitia James's civil fraud judgment against Trump. It also targeted Jan. 6 prosecutions and DOJ actions against anti-abortion protesters. The group was directed to provide quarterly reports directly to the White House — an extraordinary breach of DOJ independence. A separate Bondi directive required all DOJ career attorneys to provide zealous advocacy for Trump administration policies, threatening termination for refusals. Legal scholars characterized the working group as itself a weaponization of DOJ, using institutional power to reverse accountability for the sitting president while targeting his prior accusers.

sources.title: US Justice Department 'weaponization' reviews spark calls to drop prosecutions

title: DOGE Seeks Access to IRS Taxpayer Data on All Americans
synopsis: In February 2025, Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency sought access to the IRS's Integrated Data Retrieval System — a heavily protected database containing the financial records, tax returns, Social Security numbers, bank account details, and employment information of every taxpayer, business, and nonprofit in the country. DOGE software engineer Gavin Kliger was set to be granted access imminently, according to IRS sources. Democratic Senators Ron Wyden and Elizabeth Warren wrote to the acting IRS Commissioner calling the proposal weaponization of taxpayer data. The move came alongside DOGE already having penetrated Treasury Department payment systems, Social Security Administration records, and at least seven other major agency databases. A Washington Post investigation found DOGE had secured access to competitors' trade secrets and nonpublic regulatory data at those agencies. Privacy advocates warned the consolidation of data from multiple agencies in DOGE's hands had no legal precedent.

sources.title: DOGE seeks access to highly sensitive taxpayer data at IRS | CNN Politics

title: Trump Fires Head of Whistleblower Protection Agency
synopsis: In February 2025, Trump fired Hampton Dellinger, head of the Office of Special Counsel — the federal agency specifically created to protect government whistleblowers from retaliation. Dellinger, appointed by Biden in 2024 and confirmed by the Senate to a five-year term, sued, calling his removal unlawful. U.S. District Judge Amy Berman Jackson temporarily reinstated him on February 10, and on March 2 ruled his firing unlawful and issued a permanent injunction, finding Trump had violated federal law. The Trump administration rushed to appeal. The firing was widely interpreted as an attempt to eliminate the very agency that could shield employees reporting misconduct from retaliation, effectively clearing the way for agencies to punish internal dissenters without oversight. It followed a broader pattern of retaliatory action — including EPA firing at least 8 employees who signed a dissent letter in August 2025, and FEMA placing 21 employees on leave after they cosigned a critical open letter.

sources.title: Judge orders fired head of whistleblower agency reinstated while fight continues over Trump removal | AP News

title: Trump DOJ Indicts James Comey and Letitia James on Political Charges
synopsis: On September 25, 2025, a federal grand jury indicted former FBI Director James Comey on two charges of lying to Congress, in a case filed days after Trump publicly appeared to demand prosecution of longtime foes. On October 9, 2025, a Trump-handpicked prosecutor named Lindsey Halligan — an insurance lawyer with zero prior prosecutorial experience who was previously part of Trump's personal legal team — secured an indictment of New York Attorney General Letitia James on bank fraud charges related to a home purchase, after Trump publicly called for her prosecution on Truth Social. The original U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia resigned under pressure to prosecute James. On November 24, 2025, a federal judge dismissed both indictments, ruling that Halligan had been illegally appointed and lacked authority to bring charges. The episode was described by the New York Times as the most direct intervention in the justice system since the Nixon era.

sources.title: Read the Trump administration's full indictment of former FBI Director Comey | PBS News

title: DOGE Deploys Musk Grok AI on Sensitive Federal Government Data
synopsis: By May 2025, DOGE teams were using a customized version of Elon Musk's Grok artificial intelligence chatbot — built by his company xAI — to analyze sensitive federal government data at the Department of Homeland Security and potentially other agencies, according to Reuters reporting based on three sources. The deployment occurred without proper agency approval and raised potential violations of conflict-of-interest laws, as Musk stood to benefit commercially from his AI product gaining government contracts and exposure to federal datasets. DOGE had by this point accumulated access to data across at least seven major departments. Experts warned that using Musk's proprietary commercial AI on government data gave xAI a potential competitive advantage over rivals and exposed sensitive personal information on millions of Americans to a privately-held company owned by the head of DOGE itself — a person simultaneously running Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI while serving as a de facto senior government official.

sources.title: Exclusive: Musk’s DOGE expanding his Grok AI in US government, raising conflict concerns | Reuters

title: AP Banned from White House Over Gulf of Mexico Refusal
synopsis: Beginning February 11, 2025, the Trump White House barred Associated Press reporters and photographers from Oval Office events, Air Force One, and presidential pool coverage — all because AP declined to follow Trump's executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. AP chief photographer Evan Vucci testified in federal court on March 27 that the ban left the wire service basically dead in the water on major news stories. U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden — a Trump appointee — issued a preliminary injunction on April 8 ordering access restored, writing that under the First Amendment, if the Government opens its doors to some journalists, it cannot then shut those doors to other journalists because of their viewpoints. The White House defied the order on April 14, barring AP reporters from an Oval Office event with El Salvador's president. The administration appealed the ruling and continued selective exclusions for months. The AP's lawsuit, filed February 2025, marked the first time a major wire service had been forced to sue the U.S. government for press access in modern history. Forty press associations issued a joint condemnation of the White House's conduct.

sources.title: AP journalists barred from Air Force One over 'Gulf of Mexico' naming dispute | PBS News

title: White House Seizes Control of Presidential Press Pool from WHCA
synopsis: On February 25, 2025, press secretary Karoline Leavitt announced the White House would assume direct control over which journalists participate in the presidential press pool — ending nearly a century of tradition in which the independent White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) managed pool rotations. Leavitt stated: For decades a group of DC-based journalists — the White House Correspondents Association — has dictated which journalists get to ask questions of the President. Not anymore. The same evening, HuffPost and Reuters were removed from the February 26 pool manifest and replaced with Newsmax and Blaze Media. WHCA President Eugene Daniels warned: This move tears at the independence of a free press. It suggests the government will choose its own press corps. New York Times chief White House reporter Peter Baker compared the move to Vladimir Putin taking control of Russia's Kremlin press corps. AP, Reuters, and Bloomberg issued a joint statement warning the change threatened democracy. The unprecedented power grab was condemned by dozens of press freedom organizations as a direct mechanism for government control of who witnesses and reports on the presidency.

sources.title: White House takes control of the press pool covering Trump

title: Wire Services Stripped of Permanent White House Pool Slots
synopsis: On April 15, 2025 — one day after a court ordered AP's access restored — the White House announced it was eliminating the permanent press pool slot for wire services, ending decades of guaranteed rotation for AP, Reuters, and Bloomberg News. Under the new policy, wire services would compete for one rotating spot among approximately 30 print and newspaper outlets, effectively diluting their access to the president. Reuters, AP, and Bloomberg had collectively reached billions of people worldwide through their pool-based presidential coverage. The WHCA condemned the change as continued retaliation for independent editorial decisions. AP immediately filed in federal court, arguing the new policy was a deliberate attempt to circumvent Judge McFadden's April 8 injunction restoring its access. On May 12, 2025, all three wire services were excluded from the press pool accompanying Trump on Air Force One to Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the UAE — the first time major international wire services had been barred from a U.S. presidential foreign trip in modern history. The White House separately suppressed at least two pool reports in early April by declining to distribute them through official channels, including one noting AP journalists had been turned away from a presidential dinner.

sources.title: White House takes control of the press pool covering Trump

title: Trump Dismantles Voice of America, Fires 1,300 Journalists
synopsis: On March 14, 2025, President Trump signed an executive order gutting the U.S. Agency for Global Media (USAGM), Voice of America's parent. By the morning of March 15, all 1,300 VOA employees had been placed on paid administrative leave, barred from the building and their equipment. DOGE operative Gavin Kliger — a former Twitter engineer — had been spotted inside VOA headquarters weeks earlier. VOA director Michael Abramowitz stated: For the first time in 83 years, the storied Voice of America is being silenced. Kari Lake, Trump's loyalist USAGM adviser, signed termination notices and canceled the agency's 15-year lease. VOA had operated continuously since 1942, originally to counter Nazi propaganda, and reached an estimated 247 million people weekly in 47 languages. Russian state media celebrated the shutdown; China's state press called VOA a dirty rag. The National Press Club said the action undermines America's long-standing commitment to a free press. Courts had blocked similar USAGM dismantlement attempts during Trump's first term. The shutdown left audiences across authoritarian states without access to independent, U.S.-funded journalism precisely when such coverage mattered most.

sources.title: Voice of America channels fall silent as Trump administration guts agency and cancels contracts | CNN Business

title: Radio Free Europe and Radio Free Asia Grants Terminated
synopsis: On March 15, 2025, simultaneous with the VOA shutdown, the Trump administration terminated federal grants to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), Radio Free Asia (RFA), and the Middle East Broadcasting Networks. RFE/RL had been founded in 1950 to counter Soviet propaganda and broadcasts to countries including Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, and Central Asia. RFA broadcasts to China, North Korea, and Southeast Asia. RFE/RL president Steve Capus said the termination would be a massive gift to America's enemies, many of whom are already celebrating. RFA president Bay Fang called it a reward to dictators and despots, including the Chinese Communist Party. Czech Republic Foreign Minister Jan Lipavský immediately sought EU backing to maintain RFE/RL operations from its Prague headquarters. USAGM's funding terminations had Kari Lake's signature. A senior official at one of the networks told NPR: We would bleed out. Prior funding freeze attempts during Trump's first term had been halted by courts. Russian and Chinese state propaganda celebrated the grant terminations. The combined networks had reached over 420 million people weekly across more than 100 countries in 63 languages.

sources.title: Radio Free Asia halting news operations due to funding woes | AP News

title: FCC Revives Broadcast License Complaints Against ABC, CBS, NBC
synopsis: On January 22, 2025 — two days after inauguration — new FCC Chairman Brendan Carr resurrected three broadcaster complaints that his predecessor Jessica Rosenworcel had dismissed as seeking to weaponize the licensing authority of the FCC in a way that is fundamentally at odds with the First Amendment. The revived complaints targeted ABC (over its September 2024 presidential debate moderation), CBS (over 60 Minutes' editing of a Kamala Harris interview), and NBC (over equal-time issues with Saturday Night Live). Carr declined to revive a simultaneous Fox complaint. By mid-2025, Carr had launched formal investigations of nearly every major broadcast network — ABC, CBS, NBC, NPR, and PBS — with Fox the sole exception. Democrat FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez said the investigations represented the agency acting as the president's speech police. The investigations served as leverage in regulatory proceedings: CBS parent Paramount settled Trump's $10 billion lawsuit for $16 million in July 2025, after which Carr approved the Paramount-Skydance merger within weeks. Trump openly called on Carr to revoke licenses, stating on Air Force One in September 2025 that Carr is a patriot who would decide if networks should have their licenses taken away.

sources.title: Trump calls for FCC to revoke ABC and NBC licenses : NPR

title: CBS Pays Trump $16M to Settle 60 Minutes Lawsuit, Merger Approved
synopsis: On July 2, 2025, CBS parent company Paramount Global agreed to pay $16 million — to Trump's future presidential library, plus legal fees — to settle his lawsuit over 60 Minutes' editing of a Kamala Harris interview. Legal experts widely characterized the case as meritless; the edit had trimmed Harris's answer for time, a standard broadcast practice. The settlement was made while Paramount was seeking FCC approval to sell itself to Skydance Media, bankrolled by Oracle founder Larry Ellison, a Trump ally. FCC Chairman Carr had initiated a formal review of the 60 Minutes complaint, creating regulatory leverage. Shortly after settlement, the FCC approved the merger. CBS also announced it would release future interview transcripts of presidential candidates and hired a former Trump-nominated official as a news ombudsman at Skydance's demand. Employees held an emergency staff meeting described as widespread distress. Senator Elizabeth Warren called the settlement bribery in plain sight. FCC Democrat Anna Gomez called it a desperate move to appease the Administration. Knight First Amendment Institute director Jameel Jaffer said the $16 million payment had negligible legal basis and that Trump's presidential library will be a permanent monument to Paramount's surrender.

sources.title: Paramount settles Trump’s ‘60 Minutes’ lawsuit with $16 million payout and no apology | CNN Business

title: ABC Pays Trump $15M Over Stephanopoulos Comment, Sets Chilling Precedent
synopsis: In January 2025, Walt Disney Co., parent of ABC News, agreed to pay $15 million to Trump's presidential foundation plus $1 million in legal fees to settle a defamation lawsuit filed by Trump against anchor George Stephanopoulos. Stephanopoulos had inaccurately described the verdict in E. Jean Carroll's civil lawsuit against Trump during a live broadcast. Despite the legal case being considered weak by media law scholars — as Carroll had indeed won a civil judgment finding Trump liable for sexual abuse — Disney chose settlement over litigation, issuing a note of regret. Legal experts told outlets including TIME that the settlement would produce a chilling effect, incentivizing self-censorship across newsrooms fearful of costly litigation from a sitting president with regulatory power over their broadcast licenses. Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression chief counsel Bob Corn-Revere said: A cold wind just blew through every newsroom. The precedent set by both the ABC and CBS settlements — that networks would pay millions rather than defend accurate or defensible journalism — marked what press freedom advocates called a structural shift toward corporate capitulation to government pressure, particularly when FCC regulatory approvals were simultaneously in play.

sources.title: Why ABC News settled with Donald Trump for $15 million | CNN Business

title: Trump Sues Wall Street Journal for $10B, Bans Reporter from Scotland Trip
synopsis: On July 18, 2025, Trump filed a $10 billion defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal, its parent company News Corp, publisher Almar Latour, two reporters, and owner Rupert Murdoch over a July 17 article reporting that a 2003 birthday album gifted to Jeffrey Epstein included a note bearing Trump's name with a sexually suggestive drawing. Trump denied the letter's authenticity. The following Monday, July 21, the White House used its seized control of press pool assignments to ban WSJ reporter Tarini Parti from covering Trump's four-day trip to his golf courses in Turnberry and Aberdeen, Scotland. Press secretary Karoline Leavitt cited fake and defamatory conduct. The WHCA urged the White House to restore WSJ's position. The Wall Street Journal had been a regular pool participant until the Epstein story broke. The lawsuit named Rupert Murdoch — nominally a Trump ally — illustrating that even outlets within conservative media ecosystems were not immune to retaliation. Press groups noted the chilling paradox: the president who had promised to end censorship was suing a major newspaper over a story about a convicted sex trafficker while simultaneously using presidential access control as a punitive weapon.

sources.title: Trump sues Murdoch and Wall Street Journal for $10bn over Epstein article

title: FCC Forces ABC to Suspend Jimmy Kimmel Over Charlie Kirk Monologue
synopsis: On September 17-18, 2025, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr appeared on a conservative podcast and threatened to revoke ABC affiliate broadcast licenses if they continued airing Jimmy Kimmel Live! — citing Kimmel's Monday monologue suggesting Trump supporters were exploiting the death of Charlie Kirk. Within hours of Carr's threats, Nexstar Media Group (operator of 28 ABC affiliates, with its $6.2 billion Tegna merger requiring FCC approval) announced it would preempt the show indefinitely. Sinclair Broadcast Group (38 ABC stations, also with pending FCC regulatory matters) followed. ABC parent Disney, which was seeking FCC approval for ESPN's NFL Network acquisition, then suspended Kimmel indefinitely. Trump called it Great News for America. FCC Democrat Anna Gomez said Disney had faced clear government intimidation. The ACLU, Writers Guild, SAG-AFTRA, and dozens of lawmakers condemned the suspension as government-compelled censorship. After protests in California and national outcry, Disney reinstated Kimmel on September 22. CBS had canceled The Late Show with Stephen Colbert under comparable circumstances months earlier, also coinciding with its $16 million Trump settlement and FCC merger approval. Both Colbert and Kimmel were TV's two most vocally anti-Trump late-night hosts.

sources.title: Disney's ABC pulls 'Jimmy Kimmel Live!'  after FCC chair criticizes the host's Charlie Kirk comments

title: Hegseth Bans Major Media from Pentagon, Requires Pledge Not to Report Unclassified Info
synopsis: In May 2025, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a memo imposing sweeping new restrictions on Pentagon press access, banning reporters from large swaths of the building without government escorts and requiring enhanced scrutiny of credentials. Hegseth had already evicted NPR and other outlets from their dedicated Pentagon workspaces in January 2025. In September 2025, he escalated: requiring credentialed journalists to sign a 17-page pledge not to publish information not approved for release, including unclassified information. Hegseth posted on X: The press does not run the Pentagon — the people do. More than 30 mainstream outlets — including AP, Bloomberg, Reuters, the Washington Post, CNN, and the New York Times — declined to sign and surrendered their credentials in October 2025. Pentagon briefings, once routine, became restricted to a newly credentialed press corps composed primarily of conservative outlets: One America News, The Daily Signal, Fox News, and Newsmax. On December 4, 2025, the New York Times filed a federal lawsuit against the Pentagon, arguing the rules violated First Amendment free speech and due process protections, giving Hegseth sole personal authority to ban reporters. In December, the Pentagon held orientation briefings exclusively for its favored conservative corps, with AP, Reuters, CNN, and the Post all denied access.

sources.title: Major media outlets, including Hegseth’s former employer Fox News, decline to sign new Pentagon reporting rules - POLITICO

title: Congress Defunds Corporation for Public Broadcasting, CPB Shuts Down
synopsis: In May 2025, Trump signed an executive order directing the Corporation for Public Broadcasting to cease all direct and indirect funding to NPR and PBS, calling their journalism biased and not fair. On July 24, 2025, Trump signed a $9 billion rescissions bill that clawed back $1.1 billion in congressionally appropriated CPB funding through fiscal year 2027. CPB, which had channeled federal money to over 1,500 local public radio and television stations nationwide for nearly 60 years, announced on August 1, 2025 that it was beginning to wind down operations. CPB President Patricia Harrison called it the first time in nearly six decades Congress had refused to fund the corporation. NPR, PBS, and their more than 1,500 member stations — many serving rural communities with no commercial news alternatives — faced devastating funding gaps. The FCC simultaneously investigated NPR and PBS for alleged commercialization violations under Chairman Carr. Approximately 50 million Americans already lived in news deserts in 2025 according to the Medill Local News Initiative. NPR pledged $8 million from its budget to help local stations. The shutdown represented the most comprehensive government elimination of public broadcasting infrastructure in U.S. history, undertaken as critics argued it was designed to silence journalism hostile to the administration.

sources.title: CPB to shut down after public media loses federal funding : NPR

title: AP Photojournalist Evan Vucci: White House Ban Leaves Outlet Dead in the Water
synopsis: On March 27, 2025, AP chief Washington photographer Evan Vucci testified under oath in federal court about the professional and constitutional damage caused by the Trump White House's ban on AP photojournalists. Vucci, who had photographed every major presidential moment for over a decade including the iconic 2024 Butler, Pennsylvania assassination attempt image, testified that the ban left AP really struggling to keep up with competitors at defining news events of the early Trump second term. It's hurting us big time. We're basically dead in the water on major news stories, Vucci stated. AP chief White House correspondent Zeke Miller also testified to the access restrictions' impact. AP photojournalists had been blocked from Air Force One, the Oval Office, and pool events continuously since February 11, 2025. An AP photographer was additionally barred from the West Palm Beach airport tarmac to document Air Force One's arrival. Despite a court injunction on April 8 ordering access restored, the White House again barred AP from an Oval Office event on April 14. The targeting of photojournalists — who document the visual record of the presidency — represented a specific attack on the visual historical archive of American democracy, motivated solely by the AP's refusal to rename the Gulf of Mexico in its style guide.

sources.title: He took the iconic Trump fist-pump photo. Now he’s fighting Trump to be allowed back in the Oval Office.

title: Iran Nuclear Talks Collapse After Five Rounds
synopsis: From April through May 2025, the Trump administration conducted five rounds of nuclear negotiations with Iran — the first such direct US-Iran diplomatic contact since 2017 — mediated by Oman and held in Muscat and Rome. US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff initially floated allowing Iran to enrich uranium at 3.67%, then reversed course demanding total dismantlement of all enrichment capability, which he called a red line. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called enrichment non-negotiable. By the fifth round in Rome on May 23, Oman's mediator reported some but not conclusive progress. Witkoff left early. Iran had accelerated enrichment to 60% purity, enough to produce material for over a dozen weapons within weeks. A bipartisan letter signed by 52 senators and 177 representatives warned Trump against any deal allowing Iran to retain any enrichment capability. Talks formally collapsed when Trump, frustrated with the pace, privately issued ultimatums to Tehran and then ordered military strikes without returning to negotiations, bypassing Congress entirely.

sources.title: 'Professional' fifth round of Iran nuclear talks ends without conclusion

title: Hegseth Signal Chat: Classified Yemen Strike Plans Leaked
synopsis: In March 2025, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used his personal cell phone to share sensitive operational details about planned US airstrikes against Houthi targets in Yemen via the commercial Signal messaging app — accidentally including Atlantic editor-in-chief Jeffrey Goldberg in the chat. The messages disclosed F/A-18 launch times, bomb drop schedules, drone strike windows, and Tomahawk missile timing — information drawn directly from a classified SECRET//NOFORN email sent by CENTCOM commander Gen. Michael Kurilla. Hegseth shared the same information in a second Signal chat that included his wife and brother. A December 2025 Pentagon Inspector General report found Hegseth violated Defense Department regulations and federal records law, concluding his actions created a risk to operational security that could have resulted in failed U.S. mission objectives and potential harm to U.S. pilots. The Pentagon refused to provide Hegseth's phone to investigators; many messages had auto-deleted. Trump officials including DNI Tulsi Gabbard and CIA Director John Ratcliffe denied classified material was shared.

sources.title: The Atlantic posts Signal chat with attack plans from Hegseth | AP News

title: Trump Casts Doubt on NATO Article 5 Mutual Defense Commitment
synopsis: On June 24, 2025, en route to a NATO summit in The Hague, Netherlands, President Trump publicly cast doubt on the United States' commitment to mutual defense under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty. When reporters aboard Air Force One pressed Trump on whether he remained committed to Article 5 — the cornerstone provision holding that an attack on one ally constitutes an attack on all — Trump responded: I'm committed to saving lives. I'm committed to life and safety. He conspicuously declined to reaffirm Article 5 before European allies convened to signal unity against Russian aggression. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte attempted to contain the damage, saying he had no doubt about US commitment. The Hague summit was specifically designed to deter Russian President Vladimir Putin. Congress had passed legislation in the 2024 National Defense Authorization Act prohibiting Trump from unilaterally withdrawing from the North Atlantic Treaty without a two-thirds Senate vote, reflecting bipartisan concerns about Trump's NATO reliability.

sources.title: Trump says whether he'll commit to NATO mutual defense guarantee 'depends on your definition'

title: Trump Signs $142 Billion Saudi Arms Deal, Defends MBS on Khashoggi
synopsis: During Trump's May 2025 visit to Riyadh, the US signed what the White House called the largest defense cooperation agreement in American history — a $142 billion arms package with Saudi Arabia covering air and missile defense systems, advanced fighter aircraft, maritime security technology, and space capabilities involving more than a dozen US defense companies including Lockheed Martin, RTX, Boeing, Northrop Grumman, and General Atomics. Trump simultaneously designated Saudi Arabia as a major non-NATO ally. In November 2025, when Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman visited the White House, Trump publicly contradicted US intelligence findings by asserting that MBS knew nothing about the 2018 murder of Washington Post columnist Jamal Khashoggi at the Saudi consulate in Istanbul — a killing for which US intelligence agencies had assessed MBS bore direct responsibility. The episode reflected a broader Trump administration abandonment of human rights conditions on arms sales, with the White House claiming no one cares more about human rights than Trump while waiving accountability for Khashoggi's murder.

sources.title: US and Saudi Arabia sign $142bn arms deal as Trump to meet Syrian leader | US foreign policy | The Guardian

title: Trump Ukraine Peace Plan Favors Russian Territorial Demands
synopsis: In November 2025, the Associated Press obtained a draft of Trump's Ukraine peace plan — negotiated between the Trump administration and Moscow by envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner — which would require Ukraine to cede occupied territories to Russia and limit the size of the Ukrainian military. Ukrainian officials described the proposal as decidedly favorable to Russia, which had started the war through an unprovoked invasion. The plan included a side agreement on security guarantees that explicitly did not obligate the US or European allies to intervene in the event of future Russian aggression against Ukraine. Ukrainian officials told Axios that after a five-hour Kremlin meeting between Witkoff, Kushner, and Putin, the US proposal worsened from Kyiv's perspective, with American envoys seemingly selling Russia's demand for full Donbas annexation. Trump gave Zelensky a Thanksgiving deadline to accept the plan. Zelensky said Ukraine faced an impossible choice between national dignity and losing its primary backer. Trump claimed Zelensky's negotiators love the plan while Russian officials simultaneously registered objections.

sources.title: The 'land swap' that wasn't: Inside Trump's frantic dash for Ukraine peace | Reuters

title: Trump Pressures Asian Allies to Pay for Their Own Military Protection
synopsis: Throughout 2025, Trump systematically weaponized America's military alliance commitments in Asia as leverage for trade and financial extraction, declaring Japan and South Korea should pay for their own defense. In April 2025, Trump included troop cost-sharing in tariff negotiations with both nations, posting on Truth Social that defense burden-sharing was part of one-stop shopping deals. Japan hosts approximately 50,000 US troops and South Korea 28,500 — both relying on the US nuclear umbrella against China, North Korea, and Russia. Trump told South Korea in July 2025 it should pay $10 billion annually for the US troop presence, having already extracted $350 billion in investment pledges and $150 billion in shipbuilding cooperation from Seoul, and $550 billion in US investment pledges from Tokyo. Defense experts warned Trump's transactional approach was undermining deterrence. Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi committed to raising defense spending to 2% of GDP partly to forestall US troop withdrawal threats.

sources.title: Trump includes US troop costs in tariff talks with Asian allies

title: US Begins Drawing Down Forces from Iraq Amid Iran Power Vacuum Fears
synopsis: In mid-August 2025, the US military began a phased withdrawal of its approximately 2,500 troops from Iraq under a September 2024 security agreement with Baghdad, redeploying many to neighboring Syria and others to Iraqi Kurdistan. By October 1, 2025, the Pentagon confirmed the drawdown was underway, with forces departing Ain al-Asad base in western Iraq and Baghdad. Under the agreement's timeline, most US troops were to leave Iraq proper by fall 2026, with only 250–300 advisers remaining at Ayn al-Assad Airbase in Anbar province. Security experts warned the withdrawal risked creating a power vacuum exploitable by Iran, which had spent decades embedding military, political, economic, and social influence in Iraq through IRGC-linked militias. Terrorism analyst Bill Roggio noted Iran operates on timeframes of decades and generations and the withdrawal advanced its goal of expelling US forces from the region. The timing coincided with a dramatic weakening of Iran's regional proxies following the June 2025 US-Israeli strikes.

sources.title: US military begins drawing down mission in Iraq | AP News

title: US Strikes IRGC Targets After Iran Attacks US Base in Jordan
synopsis: On July 29, 2026, following an Iranian ballistic missile attack on a US military base in Jordan that the IRGC framed as retaliation for US airstrikes killing Iranian advisers in Iraq, US Central Command launched what it described as a heavy wave of strikes against Iran, hitting dozens of IRGC targets over approximately two hours. The targets included military command centers, missile and drone production and storage facilities, coastal surveillance and defense sites, and maritime capabilities along the Strait of Hormuz. In a coordinated operation, the US partnered with Saudi Arabia to strike Iran-backed militias in Iraq, killing at least 20 fighters and 6 Iranian IRGC advisers. Trump vowed to hit Iran very hard before the strikes, publicly telegraphing the retaliation to media. The Jordan attack by Iran came as the fragile June 17 ceasefire agreement was already breaking down over repeated Strait of Hormuz confrontations. CENTCOM reported all Iranian missiles targeting US forces were intercepted. The strikes represented the latest escalatory cycle in a conflict with no clear diplomatic off-ramp, raising fears of an open-ended US military engagement.

sources.title: US launches 'heavy' strikes on Iran after attempted attack on American troops

title: DOGE Copied All 548 Million SSNs to Unsecured Cloud Without Oversight
synopsis: In August 2025, Social Security Administration Chief Data Officer Charles Borges filed a whistleblower complaint with Congress alleging that DOGE officials employed as SSA staff had copied the entire NUMIDENT database — containing 548 million Social Security numbers along with names, addresses, dates of birth, parents' names, and other identifying information for every living and dead American who ever had an SSN — to a custom Amazon Web Services cloud environment that lacked any verified security oversight. The transfer occurred after the Supreme Court's June 6, 2025 ruling lifted a lower-court injunction blocking DOGE's SSA access. The acting chief information security officer had formally flagged the request as high risk and warned it could make Americans vulnerable to identity theft, but DOGE-affiliated CIO Aram Moghaddassi and Michael Russo approved the transfer anyway, arguing the business need is higher than the security risk. No independent security monitoring was in place; no one outside the DOGE group had insight into the code being executed against live SSA production data. Borges received no response to his security concerns from DOGE-affiliated staff. The SSA's spokesperson disputed the characterization but confirmed the environment existed.

sources.title: Whistleblower says DOGE put Social Security numbers at risk : NPR

title: Supreme Court Grants DOGE Unimpeded Access to Social Security Records
synopsis: On June 6, 2025, a 6-3 Supreme Court granted the Trump administration's emergency request to lift a lower-court preliminary injunction that had blocked DOGE from accessing sensitive Social Security Administration records. The unsigned majority order provided no detailed reasoning. Liberal justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson dissented. The ruling came after U.S. District Judge Ellen Lipton Hollander of Maryland had found in April 2025 that the government never identified or articulated even a single reason for which the DOGE Team needs unlimited access to SSA's entire record systems, exposing personal, confidential, sensitive, and private information that millions of Americans entrusted to their government. Hollander's injunction had directed DOGE staffers to delete any non-anonymized SSA data in their possession and remove software they had installed on SSA systems. Several DOGE staffers had been granted access to SSA systems — including the Master Beneficiary Record, Supplemental Security Record, and Numident files — before their background checks were completed and before inter-agency detail agreements were finalized. DOGE staffer Akash Bobba had been working off-site at OPM while accessing SSA's master data warehouse, creating additional exposure risks.

sources.title: Supreme Court restores DOGE’s access to sensitive Social Security data and says it doesn’t have to turn over documents | CNN Politics

title: DOGE Staff Accessed Classified Systems Without Proper Security Clearances
synopsis: Within days of Trump's January 20, 2025 inauguration, DOGE personnel with no verified security clearances began accessing classified and sensitive government systems at the Treasury Department, USAID, the Office of Personnel Management, the Department of Energy, and other agencies. At USAID, senior security officials were placed on administrative leave for attempting to prevent DOGE from entering restricted areas housing classified intelligence reports. CIA, NSA, the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA), and CISA all expressed concerns to the White House. Intelligence Community sources told Biometric Update that background checks for even the lowest Non-Sensitive Public Trust tier — required for anyone accessing systems with sensitive personal or financial data — had not been completed for DOGE personnel and would take months. Trump had signed an executive order on January 20 allowing administration officials to grant interim top secret security clearances with minimal vetting. Senator Mark Warner and seven colleagues sent a letter demanding a list of all DOGE personnel, their clearances, and every system they had accessed. A Senate Intelligence Committee ranking member noted that clearance files for Intelligence Community personnel — which if exposed would endanger lives — were potentially accessible. Eight senators warned that DOGE's practices created significant national security and broader economic risks.

sources.title: DOGE team gain accounts on classified systems with nuclear secrets : NPR

title: Courts Find DOGE Probationary Firings Illegal; 25,000 Workers Reinstated
synopsis: By mid-March 2025, two federal judges had found the Trump administration's mass firing of probationary federal workers — totaling approximately 24,583 terminations across civilian agencies — to be illegal. On March 13, U.S. District Judge William Alsup in San Francisco issued a preliminary injunction covering employees at the Departments of Veterans Affairs, Agriculture, Defense, Energy, Interior, and Treasury, calling the firings a sham because the Office of Personnel Management had orchestrated them using a template letter falsely attributing terminations to individual performance. Alsup noted that a USDA earth sciences employee had been fired after receiving only outstanding performance reviews. Hours later, U.S. District Judge James Bredar in Maryland ordered reinstatement at 18 additional agencies. Court filings showed the IRS chief human capital officer had been told by her Treasury supervisor that 6,700 firings must take place because OPM ordered them — something she described as unprecedented in her decades of federal HR work. The administration reinstated approximately 24,570 workers but placed most on administrative leave rather than returning them to duty, which Alsup explicitly said violated his order. Multiple agencies argued reinstatement would cause significant turmoil, revealing the administration's continued resistance to judicial authority over its illegal workforce dismantling.

sources.title: Federal judge orders agencies to bring back fired probationary workers

title: Trump Demands Powell Termination to Destroy Fed Independence
synopsis: Beginning in April 2025 and escalating throughout the year, Trump launched an unprecedented campaign to politically subjugate the Federal Reserve. On April 17, 2025, Trump posted on Truth Social that Fed Chair Jerome Powell's termination cannot come fast enough, called him always TOO LATE AND WRONG, and declared in the Oval Office, If I want him out, he'll be out of there real fast, believe me. In May, he called Powell a fool and a major loser. In July, Trump made a rare visit to the Fed's Washington headquarters to wave documents alleging $2.5 billion cost overruns in a building renovation, floating this as grounds for firing Powell. Legal scholars and economists warned that any attempt to fire Powell — whose term expired May 2026 — would trigger market chaos, spike bond yields, collapse the dollar, and destroy investor confidence in U.S. financial institutions. The Fed was holding rates at 4.25%–4.5% precisely because Trump's tariffs threatened to reignite inflation. By attacking Powell for refusing to cut rates that would worsen tariff-driven inflation, Trump was effectively demanding the Fed undermine its core mandate to protect his trade war politically. Powell repeatedly stated: Our independence is a matter of law. We're not removable except for cause.

sources.title: Trump says Powell termination can't come fast enough

title: Auto Industry Hit: GM Profits Drop 35%, Ford Takes $800M Tariff Loss
synopsis: Trump's 25% tariff on all imported finished vehicles and parts, imposed in early April 2025, devastated the North American auto industry. General Motors reported a 35% drop in second-quarter 2025 profits, including a $1.1 billion direct tariff hit, and warned its full-year tariff impact could reach $4–$5 billion. Ford took an $800 million tariff hit in Q2 2025 alone. Stellantis estimated tariff costs of up to 1.5 billion euros for 2025. S&P Global Mobility projected that a third of North American vehicle production could be cut just in the first weeks after the tariffs — roughly 20,000 units per day. Anderson Economic Group calculated tariff-driven cost increases of $6,200 for small cars, $8,000 for pickup trucks, $9,000 for full-size SUVs, and up to $12,200 for electric vehicles with Chinese battery components. GM announced cutting the Oshawa, Ontario plant from three shifts to two, laying off 750 workers. Windsor's Stellantis plant alternated between reduced schedules and full shutdowns. Ford CEO Jim Farley told investors: What we're seeing is a lot of cost and a lot of chaos. Despite absorbing billions in losses, automakers held prices stable through mid-2025 to avoid customer backlash, meaning the full consumer price impact had not yet materialized.

sources.title: GM’s quarterly results illustrate the folly of tariffs

title: Melania Launches $MELANIA Memecoin Night Before Inauguration
synopsis: On the eve of Donald Trump's second inauguration, January 19, 2025, First Lady Melania Trump launched the $MELANIA memecoin through her company MKT World LLC. The coin launched while the $TRUMP token was still in freefall from its own launch days earlier, cannibalizing investor attention and causing a sharp decline in the president's coin. At peak, $MELANIA reached a market cap of approximately $1.7 billion. Critics immediately noted that the simultaneous launch by both the incoming president and first lady of competing speculative crypto instruments — timed to capitalize on inauguration hype — represented an unprecedented monetization of the presidential transition. A group of traders was found to have made approximately $100 million on $MELANIA before it went public, suggesting advance knowledge of the launch. The coin was later dragged into a crypto fraud pump-and-dump lawsuit in October 2025. By December 2025, $MELANIA was down 99% from its peak. Melania's 2025 financial disclosure showed $6,011,259 in net proceeds from NFTs and other collectibles — a massive jump from roughly $216,000 the prior year — as part of $17.2 million in total income for 2025. The dual memecoin launches scandalized presidential ethics experts who noted the incoming president was using his inauguration to pump speculative crypto assets in which he held a dominant financial interest.

sources.title: Melania Trump launches cryptocurrency ahead of Donald Trump's inauguration

title: Trump Organization Signs Deals With Foreign Governments During Presidency
synopsis: During his second term, Trump abandoned even the nominal restraints he had placed on foreign business dealings in his first term. In April 2025, two weeks before Trump's state visit to the Middle East, the Trump Organization announced a luxury golf resort partnership with Qatari Diar — a company owned by the Qatari government — plus Dar Global, a Saudi-linked international developer with close ties to the Saudi royal family. Citizens for Ethics found that during Trump's May 2025 Middle East trip, he visited three countries — Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the UAE — each with active Trump-branded developments. Dar Global, the Saudi partner, paid the Trump Organization more than $20 million in licensing fees in 2024 alone, including more than $15 million to DT Marks KSA. A UAE-linked group tied to Abu Dhabi national security advisor Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan committed a $500 million stake in World Liberty Financial — an arrangement that coincided with the Trump administration easing technology export controls on the UAE. Qatar offered Trump a Boeing 747-8 worth hundreds of millions of dollars as a gift, which Trump accepted despite Republican national security concerns. Ethics experts noted the arrangement directly violated the Foreign Emoluments Clause.

sources.title: Trump foreign licensing income surged to $59.5 million

title: Trump Posts Buy Signal Before Tariff Pause: Potential Insider Trading
synopsis: On April 9, 2025, at 9:37 a.m., President Trump posted on Truth Social: THIS IS A GREAT TIME TO BUY!!! DJT — using the ticker symbol for Trump Media & Technology Group, his majority-owned company. Less than four hours later, Trump announced a 90-day pause on nearly all global tariffs. The S&P 500 gained 9.5% by day's end, recovering approximately $4 trillion in market value — about 70% of the value destroyed over the previous four trading days. Trump Media (DJT) surged 22.67%, far outpacing the broader market, despite being a company that lost $400 million the prior year with no relation to tariff policy. Legal experts noted that Trump's post, if made while he already planned the tariff pause, would constitute trading on insider information — a federal securities violation. Government ethics law professor Kathleen Clark at Washington University said: He's sending the message that he can effectively and with impunity manipulate the market. Securities law expert Richard Painter, a former White House ethics lawyer, said people who bought when they saw the post made a lot of money and questioned whether Trump was already planning the announcement. When asked when he decided on the pause, Trump said I would say this morning. No federal investigation was opened. Trump retained approximately 53% ownership of Trump Media, meaning any stock price surge directly enriched him personally.

sources.title: 'Great time to buy:' How Trump's tip on social media made money for investors who listened | AP News

title: Trump Pardons ~1,500 Jan 6 Defendants Including Violent Rioters
synopsis: On January 20, 2025, his first day back in office, Trump signed a proclamation granting blanket clemency to all approximately 1,500 people charged or convicted for their roles in the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack. The vast majority received full, complete and unconditional pardons, while 14 leaders of the Oath Keepers and Proud Boys had their sentences commuted to time served. Among those fully pardoned were over 300 people who had pleaded guilty to assaulting or obstructing law enforcement, including 69 who admitted assaulting police with a deadly weapon. Enrique Tarrio, sentenced to 22 years for seditious conspiracy, walked free. Stewart Rhodes, the Oath Keepers founder sentenced to 18 years, was released from prison the next morning. Trump referred to the convicted rioters as hostages and patriots, framing the largest federal prosecution in DOJ history as a political witch hunt. Judges who had presided over trials expressed outrage. NPR identified dozens of pardoned defendants who had prior convictions for rape, manslaughter, domestic violence, and child pornography. The order also directed the Attorney General to dismiss all pending indictments related to January 6, instantly terminating approximately 450 open cases and erasing the work of hundreds of prosecutors and law enforcement officers who had built the cases over four years.

sources.title: Trump issues sweeping pardons for Jan. 6 rioters

title: DOJ Fires 12+ Prosecutors Who Investigated Trump
synopsis: On January 27, 2025, acting Attorney General James McHenry signed termination letters for at least 12 senior Justice Department officials who had worked on special counsel Jack Smith's federal criminal investigations of Donald Trump. The letters stated explicitly that the officials could not be trusted to faithfully implement the President's agenda because of their significant role in prosecuting the president. Separately, approximately 40 prosecutors in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia who had worked on January 6 cases were fired the same week. Acting U.S. Attorney Ed Martin simultaneously issued a memo launching a review of all January 6 prosecutions and declaring the use of the obstruction-of-an-official-proceeding statute a great failure. The DOJ also began compiling lists of FBI agents who had worked on Smith's investigations to identify candidates for termination. FBI Director Kash Patel subsequently carried out multiple purges of the bureau's senior ranks over the following months, forcing out field office leaders, senior agents, and attorneys connected to the two Trump criminal investigations. The fired prosecutors received no advance notice. Three FBI agents — Michelle Ball, Jamie Garman, and Blaire Toleman — later sued the administration in March 2025, alleging they were terminated in a retribution campaign for their work on the 2020 election investigation.

sources.title: Justice Department moves to fire at least 12 officials who investigated Trump : NPR

title: Trump Mass-Fires 17 Independent Inspectors General Overnight
synopsis: On the night of January 24, 2025 — the fourth full day of Trump's second term — the administration fired at least 17 independent federal inspectors general across major agencies including the Departments of Defense, State, Commerce, Veterans Affairs, Housing and Urban Development, Energy, and Transportation. The firings were done by email, citing only changing priorities, with no explanation and no congressional notice, in apparent violation of the Inspector General Act of 1978, which requires the president to give Congress 30 days' advance notice with specific justification before removing an inspector general. Among those fired was Defense IG Robert Storch, whose office had opened a review of SpaceX compliance. Agriculture IG Phyllis Fong had investigated Musk's Neuralink startup; Labor IG Larry Turner and Transportation IG Eric Soskin led agencies that had previously fined Musk companies. USAID IG Paul Martin was fired in February after his office released a report on consequences of dismantling the agency and had been investigating Musk-owned Starlink terminals sent to Ukraine. Eight fired IGs sued for reinstatement. On September 24, 2025, a federal judge ruled the firings unlawful but declined to reinstate the officials. A Senate investigation found the 19 fired IGs had collectively identified over $50 billion in potential savings in 2024 alone — far exceeding DOGE.

sources.title: Trump fires more than a dozen independent inspectors general | AP News

title: Trump Calls for Impeachment of Judge Boasberg Over Deportation Ruling
synopsis: On March 18, 2025, Trump publicly called for the impeachment of U.S. District Chief Judge James Boasberg on Truth Social, calling him a Radical Left Lunatic of a Judge, a troublemaker and agitator and declaring This judge should be IMPEACHED!!! The attack came after Boasberg issued a temporary restraining order on March 15 halting Trump's use of the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to rapidly deport hundreds of alleged Venezuelan gang members without due process. Boasberg ordered deportation flights that were already airborne to turn back; the administration did not comply. In a rare rebuke, Chief Justice John Roberts issued a written public statement saying that impeachment is not an appropriate response to disagreements concerning a judicial decision. Trump continued his attacks undeterred and began fundraising off the impeachment call. Elon Musk simultaneously posted repeatedly on X calling for Republican lawmakers to impeach Boasberg. The administration stonewalled Boasberg's demands for information about the flights, with a DOJ attorney repeatedly telling the judge he was not authorized to provide details — an extraordinary rebuff of a sitting federal judge. A contempt inquiry was opened and then paused for appeals. In July 2026, Republican Senator Eric Schmitt introduced legislation named the BOASBERG Act in a further attempt to curtail the judge's authority.

sources.title: Trump says federal judge who ruled against deportation orders should be impeached | PBS News

title: DOJ Indicts NY AG Letitia James on Trumped-Up Fraud Charges
synopsis: Letitia James, the New York Attorney General who had won a landmark $454 million civil fraud judgment against Trump and his companies in 2022, became a primary target of DOJ retaliation in Trump's second term. In March 2025, FHFA Director Bill Pulte — a Trump ally — referred James to the DOJ alleging she had misrepresented information on a mortgage application. Despite a five-month investigation finding insufficient evidence to indict, Trump fired U.S. Attorney Erik Siebert in September 2025 specifically for refusing to bring charges against James and Comey. Ed Martin, Trump's special attorney and Weaponization Working Group director, sent James's attorney a letter saying he would take her resignation as an act of good faith even before any charges were filed. In October 2025, Lindsey Halligan — the same unlawfully appointed prosecutor who indicted Comey — secured a grand jury indictment against James on charges of bank fraud and making false statements. James pleaded not guilty and called the charges baseless and driven by political retribution. On November 24, 2025, the same judge who dismissed the Comey case dismissed James's indictment on the same grounds: Halligan's unlawful appointment. Subsequent federal grand juries in both Norfolk and Alexandria declined to re-indict James. The DOJ appealed. The mortgage fraud investigations of both James and Schiff were themselves investigated for potential DOJ misconduct.

sources.title: Trump and 18 allies charged in Georgia election meddling | AP News

title: Trump Accidentally Posts Private Message to Bondi Demanding Enemy Prosecutions
synopsis: On September 20, 2025, Trump posted a lengthy message on Truth Social that had been intended as a private direct message to Attorney General Pam Bondi — but was accidentally posted publicly. In it, Trump addressed Bondi directly as Pam and demanded action against his political adversaries: What about Comey, Adam Shifty Schiff, Leticia??? They're all guilty as hell, but nothing is going to be done. We can't delay any longer, it's killing our reputation and credibility. He concluded with: They impeached me twice, and indicted me (5 times!), OVER NOTHING. JUSTICE MUST BE SERVED, NOW!!! According to NBC News, Trump was surprised to discover he had published the message publicly and tried to shrug it off. The post directly contradicted Trump's repeated public claims that he did not involve himself in DOJ charging decisions. In the weeks following the post, both Comey and James were indicted. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the conduct the path to a dictatorship. Senator Adam Schiff, who was named in the post, said Trump was using the DOJ to go after his political enemies and protect his political friends. Trump later told reporters he had nothing to do with the Comey case, directly contradicting the documentary record of his own post.

sources.title: Trump accidentally posted message pressuring Pam Bondi to charge his enemies, source says

title: DOJ Vacates Oath Keepers and Proud Boys Seditious Conspiracy Convictions
synopsis: In April 2026, the Trump DOJ moved to vacate the convictions of Oath Keepers founder Stewart Rhodes and other seditious conspiracy defendants who had received sentence commutations but not pardons in January 2025. This reversed the Biden-era DOJ's landmark victories in the largest and most serious prosecutions stemming from January 6. U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta, who had overseen the trials, reluctantly granted the motion but wrote a stinging rebuke, stating the government asks to absolve these Defendants of crimes against the United States itself without alleging insufficient evidence or prosecutorial misconduct. In July 2026, Judge Timothy Kelly similarly dismissed the seditious conspiracy cases against Proud Boys leaders Ethan Nordean, Joseph Biggs, Zachary Rehl, and Dominic Pezzola, writing no one should mistake the Court's granting of the Government's motion for its agreement with those decisions and calling January 6 a perilous event and an attack on a coordinate branch of government. On August 5, 2026, Mehta dismissed the final Oath Keepers indictment, writing: This is the last of the prosecutions seeking to hold accountable those responsible for the events of Jan. 6. That book is now closed... Today's epilogue diminishes the gravity of that day, denigrates the work of the prosecutors and law enforcement officers who secured these convictions, and excuses criminal acts that caused a centuries-long pillar of our democracy — the peaceful transfer of presidential power — to buckle. The court cannot write a different ending.

sources.title: Justice Department moves to dismiss Proud Boys and Oath Keepers’ seditious conspiracy convictions | CNN Politics

title: Supreme Court Guts Nationwide Injunctions, Unlocking Birthright Citizenship Order
synopsis: On June 27, 2025, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. CASA, Inc., a trio of consolidated cases that had challenged Trump's January 20, 2025 executive order purporting to end birthright citizenship for children born to undocumented or temporary-visa-holding parents — a direct challenge to the 14th Amendment's citizenship clause, which had been settled constitutional law since United States v. Wong Kim Ark in 1898. Rather than ruling on whether the order was constitutional, the Court's conservative majority, written by Justice Amy Coney Barrett, gutted the mechanism used to block the order: nationwide (universal) injunctions. The Court held that district courts likely exceeded their equitable authority under the Judiciary Act of 1789 in issuing injunctions protecting everyone, not just plaintiffs. The decision meant the birthright citizenship order could take partial effect 30 days after the ruling in states not covered by injunctions, potentially stripping U.S. citizenship from newborns whose parents were undocumented. Three dissenting justices warned the ruling endangered constitutional rights at scale. Advocates swiftly pivoted to class-action lawsuits; a new class-based nationwide injunction was issued by July 10, 2025. The Trump administration announced it would use the ruling to seek to narrow over two dozen other injunctions blocking its various executive orders. The Supreme Court took up the underlying constitutionality of the birthright citizenship order for its 2025-26 term.

sources.title: Supreme Court leaves fate of Trump birthright citizenship order unclear | AP News
